title: Meta’s $18B child-safety settlement hinges on flawed age-verification technology
summary: Meta reached an $18 billion settlement with 52 U.S. attorneys general over child-safety concerns on Instagram and Facebook. The agreement mandates sweeping design changes, including screen-time limits, muted notifications during school hours, and default privacy settings for minors. However, these measures rely on age-verification technology, which experts argue is ineffective, biased, or poses privacy risks. The settlement highlights tensions between child safety and data privacy, with critics questioning whether Meta can implement these changes without compromising user security.
key_points: Meta settled for $18 billion over child-safety lawsuits, agreeing to implement strict platform changes for minors on Instagram and Facebook.
The settlement includes default screen-time limits (2 hours/day), overnight app blocks, and muted notifications during school hours for teen accounts.
Age-verification technology, critical for enforcing these rules, is widely criticized for ineffectiveness, bias, and privacy risks (e.g., biometric scans, ID checks).
Experts debate whether age-verification methods (behavioral analysis, selfies, government IDs) can balance safety and privacy without storing sensitive data.
Meta frames the settlement as leadership in child safety but faces skepticism due to reliance on unproven technology and potential data-breach risks.
The deal may set industry norms, but its success depends on Meta’s ability to overcome technical and ethical challenges in age verification.
